title: WORD MELT
goal: Hear one charged word as sound instead of carrying its whole story.
steps:
1. Choose Charged — Choose one charged word—not a whole painful story.
2. Say Gently — Say it gently and steadily for about twenty seconds.
3. Listen Moment — Listen for the moment it becomes rhythm, mouth movement, or noise.
4. Stop Room — Stop there and look around the room.
5. Return Seen — Meaning may return; you have seen it separate once.
win: For a moment, the word became rhythm or mouth movement before its meaning returned.
supports:
• Change one cue; make the new habit easier.
• Reset after slips; interrupt the usual sequence.
• Keep replacement easy; make the old habit harder.
• Reduce easy access to triggers; add small friction.
• Expect slips and restart quickly; reset without self-criticism.
formula_flow: Choose Charged → Say Gently → Listen Moment → Stop Room → Return Seen
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid this with slurs, trauma phrases, voices, or material that escalates symptoms.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ONE INCH BEYOND EASY
goal: Stretch one existing skill slightly and let evidence—not shame—set the next challenge.
steps:
1. Select Task — Select something you can already do.
2. Increase — Increase one dimension slightly: duration, complexity, independence, or visibility.
3. Complete Version — Complete that version and mentally name the skill that carried you through.
4. Raise One Inch — Let the next challenge be earned by evidence, not demanded by shame.
win: You completed the harder version and could name the skill that carried you.
supports:
• Describe the behaviour, not yourself; name the exact mistake.
• Name the mistake; make repair smaller than self-punishment.
• Name the behaviour; choose one repair you can make.
• Drop self-punishment; separate guilt from responsibility.
• Choose one repair; do not punish yourself for learning.

safety:

Step back when challenge impairs recovery, safety, or essential functioning.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: SET THE CONVERSATION SIZE
goal: Fit the conversation to the amount you can safely handle right now.
steps:
1. Read Bandwidth — Choose your current safe bandwidth: ONE SENTENCE, THREE SENTENCES, or FULL CONVERSATION.
2. Choose Size — Name the purpose that must fit inside that size: acknowledge, request, pause, clarify, or repair.
3. Send Signal — Draft or say only the selected amount. Stop when the sentence limit is reached, even if more remains.
4. Set Reopen — Name when or under what condition the next level can reopen. If you cannot offer one, state that honestly without making a false promise.
win: You stopped at the chosen sentence limit and made the condition for reopening clear.
supports:
• Lead with the point; end with action.
• Separate facts from tone; check the request.
• Use shorter sentences when tense; keep one issue.
• Separate tone from facts; keep one issue per conversation.
• Check the agreed deadline; avoid guessing their intent.
formula_flow: Read Bandwidth → Choose Size → Send Signal → Set Reopen
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use bandwidth limits to conceal immediate danger, threats, abuse, medical urgency, or information another person needs for safety.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THEN AND NOW, NO STORY DETAILS
goal: Separate what happened then from the options available to you now.
steps:
1. Say Happened — Say, “That happened then,” without describing what happened.
2. State Current Place — State your exact present location and today's date.
3. Name Present Freedom — Name one freedom or option available now.
4. Identify Today's Help — Identify who can help in the current day.
5. End Comparison — End after one comparison and return to the room.
win: The past stayed undescribed while today's place, date, freedom, and support became explicit.
supports:
• Name the place; avoid forced memories.
• Stop if you feel less present; keep lighting comfortable.
• Hold a familiar object; feel your feet on the floor.
• Keep your eyes open if safer; contact someone you trust.
• Move gently; contact someone trusted.
formula_flow: Say Happened → State Current Place → Name Present Freedom → Identify Today's Help → End Comparison
safety:
PAUSE
Keep your eyes open. Use only present-day room, date, place and support orientation. Do not revisit memories in detail, use trauma imagery, intensify sensations, or attempt unsupervised processing. Stop for flooding, dissociation, or weakened orientation and connect with qualified human support.
This is stabilisation only, not trauma treatment.

5. End Comparison — End after one comparison and return to the room.

WIN
The past stayed undescribed while today's place, date, freedom, and support became explicit.

• Name the place; avoid forced memories.
• Stop if you feel less present; keep lighting comfortable.
• Hold a familiar object; feel your feet on the floor.
• Keep your eyes open if safer; contact someone you trust.
• Move gently; contact someone trusted.

MIND BEND
Memory can collapse time by carrying old helplessness forward — one present option proves the conditions are not identical.

Say Happened → State Current Place → Name Present Freedom → Identify Today's Help → End Comparison

SAFETY
PAUSE
Keep your eyes open. Use only present-day room, date, place and support orientation. Do not revisit memories in detail, use trauma imagery, intensify sensations, or attempt unsupervised processing. Stop for flooding, dissociation, or weakened orientation and connect with qualified human support.
This is stabilisation only, not trauma treatment.

title: CHANGE ONE THING, WATCH ONE FEELING
goal: Change one part of an imagined scene and see which emotion actually moves.
steps:
1. Name Pair — Name two emotions in the mixture and rate each with a simple low, medium, or high—not a number.
2. Hold Scene — Hold the scene steady. Choose only one variable to test: person, time, place, audience, or outcome.
3. Swap Variable — Imagine that one variable changed for ten seconds. Keep every other fact the same.
4. Tag Driver — Notice which emotion moved and which stayed. Tag the changed variable as a likely driver, not a final explanation.
win: Only one variable changed, revealing which feeling shifted and which stayed put.
supports:
• Avoid decisions at peak emotion; name the feeling plainly.
• Notice what changed physically; lower nearby noise.
• Check basic needs; slow physical pace.
• Notice body tension; use plain language.
• Give the feeling time to move; let intensity fall.
formula_flow: Name Pair → Hold Scene → Swap Variable → Tag Driver
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use imagined substitutions to rewrite trauma, deny facts, or continue once the scene becomes overwhelming or unreal.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WHAT IS NEW THIS LAP?
goal: Require each new thinking lap to produce something genuinely new.
steps:
1. Find Novelty — At the start of another mental cycle, state the new fact, distinction, or decision it could add.
2. Name Lap — If nothing specific appears, call the lap REPETITION and keep one short mental summary.
3. Move Sensory — Shift attention to one present sensation or practical action.
win: When no new fact, distinction, or decision appeared, the loop was named repetition and attention moved elsewhere.
supports:
• Set a stop time; name one useful action.
• Change rooms if possible; use a short timer.
• Set a clear stopping point; return to current task.
• Name one action; change rooms.
• Use your hands; shift attention outward.
formula_flow: Find Novelty → Name Lap → Move Sensory
safety:
PAUSE
Return when new evidence actually arrives, not merely because discomfort returns.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: TWO CHAIRS, NO TELEPATHY
goal: Imagine both sides of a conversation without pretending you can know the other mind.
steps:
1. Picture Positions — Imagine two positions facing each other in your mind.
2. Speak Position — State your own position in first person.
3. Shift View — Imagine the other position and answer without pretending you know their mind.
4. Return To Facts — Come back to your view and separate facts from guesses.
win: Your position, their possible position, and the observable facts ended in separate places.
supports:
• Reset after slips; change the environment.
• Replace one response; notice the trigger.
• Change one cue; expect slips and restart quickly.
• Add small friction; keep replacement easy.
• Change the environment first; move the cue.
formula_flow: Picture Positions → Speak Position → Shift View → Return To Facts
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid this alone for traumatic relationships or if role-switching feels disorganising.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: TELL IT AT THE SPEED OF SAFETY
goal: Share difficult material at a pace set by safety, facts, and the support you actually want.
steps:
1. Choose Trustworthy — Choose a trustworthy listener and agree on time, confidentiality, and a stop signal.

title: MAKE FEAR NAME A DEADLINE
goal: Make fear state exactly what should happen, by when, and how confident it is.
steps:
1. Pin Forecast — Restate the fear as one visible or audible prediction—not a vague catastrophe.
2. Set Clock — Give the prediction a real time window.
3. Score Odds — Set confidence on a 0–100 scale before checking anything.
4. Observe Safely — Use only a naturally occurring safe observation; never manufacture a test.
5. Update Odds — Use the result to update confidence in either direction.
win: The prediction gained a visible outcome, deadline, and pre-check confidence that could later move with naturally occurring evidence.
supports:
• Separate guess from evidence; look for one missing fact.
• Check the whole situation; question absolute words.
• Test the assumption; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Ask what else could fit; check what you actually know.
• Use a real example; ask what would disprove it.
formula_flow: Pin Forecast → Set Clock → Score Odds → Observe Safely → Update Odds
safety:
PAUSE
Do not test danger, invade privacy, or repeat the observation to chase certainty.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: GROUNDING ANCHOR RELAY
goal: Rotate through several grounding channels and keep the one that restores the clearest present contact.
steps:
1. Select Different — Select four anchors from different systems: visual line, distant sound, contact pressure, joint position.
2. Switch Getting — Spend a short interval with each and switch before getting used to it empties it.
3. Finish Channel — Finish on the channel that restored the clearest present contact.
win: Visual, auditory, pressure, and joint cues were tested before one channel became the final anchor.
supports:
• Notice temperature and texture; slow your physical pace.
• Track one texture; feel the chair.
• Return to one real sound; touch a stable surface.
• Feel your feet; keep eyes open.
• Hear one real sound; name three visible objects.
formula_flow: Select Different → Switch Getting → Finish Channel
safety:
PAUSE
Use fewer anchors if switching itself increases overload.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE FEELING UNDER THE FEELING ABOUT IT
goal: Separate the first emotion from the emotion you are having about having it.
steps:
1. Name Emotion — Spot the primary emotion and its trigger.
2. Finish About — Then finish: ‘About feeling this, I feel…’ Locate each in a different body area or colour.
3. State Needs — Offer the primary state what it needs before addressing shame, anger, or fear about having it.
win: The primary feeling received attention before shame, anger, or fear about that feeling took over.
supports:
• Eat, drink, or rest if needed; slow physical pace.
• Let intensity fall; check basic needs.
• Use simple words for the problem; notice body tension.
• Name the emotion; wait before sending messages.
• Use plain language; name the feeling plainly.

safety:
PAUSE
Seek help if peeling exposes overwhelming trauma or self-attack.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: HALF-SPEED THE FIRST MOVE
goal: Slow only the first urge-linked movement and decide whether the next movement should happen.
steps:
1. Identify Earliest — Catch the first movement linked to the urge—turning, reaching, standing, typing.
2. Observe Direction — Do only that movement at half speed while observing its direction and tension.
3. Pause Completion — Pause at completion and decide whether the second movement serves you.
win: The initial reach, turn, stand, or type finished at half speed and ended in a fresh choice point.
supports:
• Make access harder; remember urges peak and fall.
• Drink some water; make access less convenient.
• Do one incompatible activity; move away from the cue.
• Tell someone early; delay acting for ten minutes.
• Leave the trigger; change locations.
formula_flow: Identify Earliest → Observe Direction → Pause Completion
safety:

title: DISASSEMBLE THE ALARM PANEL
goal: Change only the quietest safe channel of body alarm and leave the louder ones alone.
steps:
1. Read Channels — Read three channels without searching your whole body: SPEED, PRESSURE, and TEMPERATURE. Use lower, medium, or high.
2. Pick Smallest — Choose the safest channel with the lowest intensity. Do not pick the loudest one.
3. Move Dial — Move only that channel one step: slow one hand movement, soften one contact point, or adjust one safe layer of warmth or coolness.
4. Check Panel — Check whether that channel changed at all. Let the other two channels remain exactly as they are.
win: Speed, pressure, and temperature were read separately, then one lower-intensity channel moved a single step.
supports:
• Wait out the surge; reduce extra stimulation.
• Unclench your jaw; sit somewhere safe.
• Avoid symptom searching; use ordinary surroundings.
• Loosen your shoulders; stop body scanning.
• Avoid repeated pulse checking; sip water if it helps.
formula_flow: Read Channels → Pick Smallest → Move Dial → Check Panel
safety:
PAUSE
New, severe, or unusual physical symptoms require medical assessment. Stop for pain, faintness, breathing difficulty, confusion, or loss of orientation.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: BLANK THE NAMEPLATE
goal: Make one decision without consulting the identity label you usually use to predict yourself.
steps:
1. Picture Identity — Picture the identity label on a removable card and turn it face down.
2. Decision — For the next decision, refer only to capacities, needs, facts, and values.
3. Choose Shift — Choose.
4. Uncover Name — Then uncover the label and compare what it would have predicted.
win: Capacities, needs, facts, and values made the choice before the nameplate was turned face-up again.
supports:
• Add the missing context; ask what would disprove it.
• Ask what else could fit; use a real example.
• Avoid treating guesses as facts; check the whole situation.
• Test the assumption; question absolute words.
• Separate possibility from probability; look for one missing fact.

title: EXIST FOR ONE MINUTE WITHOUT AUTOBIOGRAPHY
goal: Spend one minute in direct experience without using your biography to explain who is here.
steps:
1. Don't Recall — For sixty seconds, do not recall name, history, status, or plans.
2. Stay Changing — Stay with changing sound, pressure, light, and movement.
3. Simple — Notice the simple ongoing sense of being present through those changes.
4. End Reclaim — Reclaim your biography on purpose at the end.
win: Sound, pressure, light, and movement continued while name, status, history, and plans stayed temporarily offline.
supports:
• Separate possibility from probability; delay the verdict.
• Question absolute words; check another angle.
• Use a real example; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Separate guess from evidence; use current facts.
• Ask what would disprove it; check what you actually know.

safety:

title: RETURN THEIR ACTION; KEEP YOUR CHOICE
goal: Keep their behaviour, what you learned, and what you choose now in separate boxes.
steps:
1. Imagine Three Boxes — Imagine three boxes: THEIR BEHAVIOUR; WHAT I LEARNED; WHAT I CHOOSE NOW.
2. Keep Each Part — Keep each thought in the right box.

title: MEMORY REVIEW BY APPOINTMENT ONLY
goal: Review a recurring memory only at a chosen time and only for a useful reason.
steps:

2. Add Keyword — When the memory loop appears outside it, add one keyword to a mental note and redirect to the present activity.

win: Outside the window, one keyword was enough; at the appointment, the memory was either processed on purpose or cancelled.
supports:
• Expect slips and restart quickly; remove easy access.
• Reset without self-criticism; keep replacement easy.
• Reduce easy access to triggers; change the environment.
• Interrupt the sequence; replace one response.
• Notice the trigger; interrupt the usual sequence.

title: MATCH THE TASK TO THE BODY’S TEMPERATURE
goal: Choose work that matches the body's current activation instead of fighting the temperature.
steps:
1. Read Body — Read current body alarm as lower, middle, or high.
2. Select Work — Select work with matching demand: energising movement for low, steady production for medium, simple contained tasks for high.
3. Reassess — Reassess after one unit and change lanes if needed.
win: Lower, middle, or high alarm was matched to a fitting task, then reassessed after one unit.
supports:
• Sit somewhere safe; use ordinary surroundings.
• Sip water if it helps; unclench your jaw.
• Reduce extra stimulation; wait out the surge.
• Keep movements gentle; give the surge time to pass.
• Avoid symptom searching; keep your body supported.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not treat serious fatigue or agitation as a productivity puzzle.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE VERSION THAT STILL COUNTS
goal: Finish the smallest version that still serves the task's essential purpose.
steps:
1. Name Task — Name the task’s essential purpose.
2. Remove Feature — Remove every feature not required for that purpose.
3. Build Smallest — Build the smallest deliverable that still works, submit or finish it, then upgrade only if time and value justify the addition.
win: Nonessential features were removed and a usable deliverable existed before any optional upgrade.
supports:
• Ship useful work; ask what is actually required.
• Leave minor flaws alone; limit checking passes.
• Follow the brief; set finish time.
• Stop low-value changes; limit checking.
• Separate important errors from polish; define good enough first.

safety:
PAUSE
Maintain full standards for safety-critical, clinical, legal, or hard to undo work.

title: TAKE UP 5% MORE SPACE

steps:
1. Widen Feet — Widen feet, elbows, chest, or seating position by a small manageable amount.
2. Keep Change — Keep the change below performance or dominance.
3. Observe Shape — Observe what the expanded shape signals internally and which words become easier to access.
win: A small increase in physical space changed the internal signal without becoming dominance or performance.
supports:
• Lower stimulation for a minute; rest before deciding.
• Wait before sending messages; eat, drink, or rest if needed.
• Check the facts separately; slow physical pace.
• Check basic needs; use simple words for the problem.
• Give the feeling time to move; notice body tension.

safety:
PAUSE

This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: UNWIND IN REVERSE
goal: Release a tension chain in the reverse order that it built.
steps:
1. Recall Muscle — Recall which muscle group tightened last.
2. Soften Work — Soften it first, then work back toward the first area that braced.
3. Pause Handoff — Pause between groups to feel the handoff.
4. Finish Original — Finish at the original starting point and compare the whole chain.
win: Each muscle group handed the release onward until you could compare the original bracing point with its starting state.
supports:
• Unclench your jaw and shoulders; keep your body supported.
• Avoid symptom searching; reduce extra stimulation.
• Let breaths happen; keep movements gentle.
• Sit somewhere safe; reduce caffeine.
• Wait out the surge; stop body scanning.

safety:
PAUSE

title: FIND FIVE COLOURS WITHOUT CHASING THEM
goal: Find five colours without using preference to pull you toward or away from them.
steps:
1. Keep Body — Keep your body still enough for safety and locate five distinct colours across the scene.
2. Name Shade — Name shade and location, not emotional meaning.
3. Don't Move — Do not move toward pleasant colours or away from unpleasant ones.
4. Finish Colour — Finish with the colour farthest from the trigger.
win: Shade and location stayed factual, and attention finished on the colour farthest from the trigger.
supports:

• Notice three colours; hear one real sound.
• Notice where your body is supported; name today's date.
• Keep your eyes on something steady; slow your physical pace.
• Feel your feet; track one texture.

title: LET ONE TASTE FINISH
goal: Let one taste complete its full life before adding another.

2. Track Taste — Track taste from first contact through peak, transformation, and complete disappearance.
3. Don't Add — Do not add another until the original flavour has ended.

win: Flavour moved from first contact through peak and disappearance, revealing when wanting continued after tasting ended.
supports:
• Feel your feet; notice temperature and texture.
• Keep eyes open; look around slowly.
• Slow your physical pace; name today's date.
• Return to one real sound; feel both feet.
• Name three visible objects; feel the chair.

title: THE ROOM HAS JOBS, NOT DEMANDS
goal: Keep only the room function that supports the next safe action and dismiss the rest for now.
steps:
1. Imagine Four Things — Picture four ordinary things from a familiar room.
2. Name Jobs — Give each only its basic job: support, light, hold, open.
3. Drop Demands — Say NOT NEEDED NOW to every function irrelevant to this moment.
4. Choose Helper — Keep only the imagined function that supports your next safe action.
win: Ordinary objects returned to simple jobs, leaving one useful function active instead of a room full of demands.
supports:
• Start with one minute; begin with the easiest part.
• Start smaller; use one window.
• Use two minutes; remove one barrier.
• Shrink the first action; set a two-minute timer.
• Remove one obvious distraction; choose a rough beginning.
formula_flow: Imagine Four Things → Name Jobs → Drop Demands → Choose Helper
safety:
PAUSE
Stop for visual pain, dizziness, nausea, disorientation, compulsive scanning, or any real emergency requiring immediate action.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

GOAL
Keep only the room function that supports the next safe action and dismiss the rest for now.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Imagine Four Things — Picture four ordinary things from a familiar room.
2. Name Jobs — Give each only its basic job: support, light, hold, open.
3. Drop Demands — Say NOT NEEDED NOW to every function irrelevant to this moment.
4. Choose Helper — Keep only the imagined function that supports your next safe action.

WIN
Ordinary objects returned to simple jobs, leaving one useful function active instead of a room full of demands.

• Start with one minute; begin with the easiest part.
• Start smaller; use one window.
• Use two minutes; remove one barrier.
• Shrink the first action; set a two-minute timer.
• Remove one obvious distraction; choose a rough beginning.

MIND BEND

Imagine Four Things → Name Jobs → Drop Demands → Choose Helper

SAFETY
PAUSE
Stop for visual pain, dizziness, nausea, disorientation, compulsive scanning, or any real emergency requiring immediate action.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ISSUE THE DECISION RECEIPT
goal: Give a completed decision a receipt so doubt has a specific rule for reopening it.
steps:
1. Picture Decision — Picture the decision, main reason, date, one simple action, review date, and conditions that justify reopening.
2. Seal — Seal it in your mind.
3. Return Reopening — When doubt returns, compare it with the reopening conditions instead of arguing the decision again from emotion.
win: Reason, date, action, review point, and reversal conditions stayed recorded instead of being rebuilt from mood.
supports:
• Silence nonessential notifications; take a real screen break.
• Finish or park one open loop; reduce background noise.
• Mute alerts; take a short break.
• Protect one focus block; return after interruptions.
• Keep one task visible; return to one target.

title: GIVE THE THOUGHT A RETURN ADDRESS
goal: Route a returning concern to one real destination or mark it undeliverable.
steps:
1. Assign Concern — Assign the concern to one place: a named person, calendar slot, document, task name, or deliberate release.
2. Route Address — Say the address in your mind and route the thought there each time it returns.
3. Mark Undeliverable — If no useful address exists, mark the thought UNDELIVERABLE and let it pass without rerouting.
win: The thought had a person, time, document, task, release point, or no valid address at all.
supports:
• Use a short focus block; return to one target.
• Choose one target; clear visual clutter.
• Reduce nearby noise; protect one focus block.
• Use one window at a time; keep one task visible.
• Park secondary tasks; take a real screen break.

title: PUT THE PROMISE AT THE CROSSROADS
goal: Place one short cue exactly where you usually begin renegotiating the decision.
steps:
1. Identify Crossroads — Find the exact moment where the decision usually changes direction.
2. Set Inner Cue — Create a short mental cue that names the action you want there.
3. Rehearse — Picture reaching the crossroads and hearing the cue once.
4. Follow Through — When the moment arrives, use the cue before renegotiation begins.
win: The crossroads arrived and the planned cue spoke before the old bargaining sequence could begin.
supports:
• Start with one minute; prepare the task in advance.
• Remove one barrier; reward starting, not finishing.
• Use a visible cue; begin while unsure.
• Touch the first item; open only what you need.
• Enter through easy work; lower the quality bar.

title: HARVEST THE PROOF OF PROGRESS
goal: Use concrete evidence of past progress to justify the next realistic step.
steps:
1. Create Prior — Collect three concrete differences created by prior effort—speed, quality, recovery time, knowledge, frequency, distance.
2. Date Examples — Attach dates or examples.
3. Choose Action — Select the one doable step that becomes reasonable because one difference now exists.
win: Three dated differences made one currently doable action feel earned by evidence rather than optimism.
supports:
• Lower the quality bar; prepare the task in advance.
• Start physically; begin with the easiest part.
• Set a two-minute timer; cut the task.
• Start with one minute; lower the first demand.
• Make the first move tiny; use one window.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not cherry-pick progress to ignore deteriorating health or strategy.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FIVE CLUES MAY BE ONE CLUE
goal: Collapse repeated clues that all came from the same source before judging how much evidence you have.
steps:
1. Name Clues — Name up to five clues currently supporting the worried conclusion.
2. Link Sources — Imagine a line between clues that came from the same person, event, article, assumption, mood, or repeated retelling.
3. Collapse Copies — Collapse every linked cluster into one source family; do not count its echoes separately.
4. Recheck Claim — Recheck the claim using the number and quality of independent families that remain.
win: Echoes from one person, event, article, assumption, mood, or retelling became a single source family.
supports:
• Make the old habit harder; keep replacement easy.
• Expect slips and restart quickly; use the same replacement repeatedly.
• Delay the routine; make the new habit easier.
• Change one cue; reset after slips.
• Remove easy access; change the environment.
formula_flow: Name Clues → Link Sources → Collapse Copies → Recheck Claim
safety:
PAUSE
Do not collapse separate danger signs or ignore qualified medical, legal, financial, or safety evidence.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ONE LOCAL REASON
goal: Find one reason within the next day that deserves ten minutes of your behaviour.
steps:
1. Find Anchor — Search only within the next twenty-four hours for one person, place, promise, task, or act that matters.

3. Invest Time — Give it ten minutes of undivided behaviour.
win: A nearby person, place, promise, task, or act received undivided time because its local meaning was clear.

• Rest before deciding; check basic needs.
• Avoid decisions at peak emotion; delay the message.
• Lower nearby noise; check the facts separately.
• Give the feeling time to move; use plain language.
• Separate feeling from fact; name the emotion.

title: CARRY FORWARD WITHOUT CALLING IT GOOD
goal: Carry forward one boundary, skill, loyalty, or value without calling the harmful event good.
steps:
1. State Clearly — State clearly what was wrong or unwanted.
2. Name Boundary — Then name one boundary, skill, loyalty, or value you can carry forward without claiming the event was beneficial.
3. Let Value — Let the value belong to you, not to the harm.
win: The event stayed wrong while something useful was reclaimed as yours rather than credited to the harm.
supports:
• Keep consequences realistic; offer only genuine options.
• Offer alternatives only if genuine; keep the limit simple.
• Decide your limit before answering; notice resentment early.
• Use a short no; take time before saying yes.
• Repeat the same wording calmly; protect your capacity.
formula_flow: State Clearly → Name Boundary → Let Value
safety:
PAUSE
Do not force lessons before grief or shock has space.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE LAST-DAY FILTER
goal: Use the end-of-life view only to rank what deserves a place today.
steps:
1. Imagine Back — Imagine looking back from life’s end—not to frighten yourself, but to rank.
2. Demand — Which current demand disappears.
3. Remain Relationship — Which relationship, integrity choice, health need, or contribution remains.
4. Give Surviving — Give the surviving priority one concrete slot today.
win: A demand lost importance while one relationship, integrity, health, or contribution priority gained a concrete time slot.
supports:
• Set a deadline; commit once chosen.
• Set a decision deadline; accept one trade-off.
• Reduce the options; choose by the strongest evidence.
• Pick the reversible option first; avoid reopening without new facts.
• Use strongest evidence; limit the options.

safety:
PAUSE
Skip mortality reflection when it intensifies anxiety, grief, or self-harm thoughts.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: PAIN IS PRESENT; LIFE HAS OTHER DEPARTMENTS
goal: Let pain be one department of life while another department keeps moving.
steps:
1. Describe Hurting — Say exactly what is hurting.
2. Continue Alongside — Then name three processes continuing alongside it: caring, learning, digesting, noticing, working, resting, relating.
3. Choose Small — Choose one small action from a continuing department without denying the pain.
win: The hurt was named honestly and one continuing process—care, learning, work, rest, or connection—received a small action.
supports:
• Make the first move tiny; lower the quality bar.
• Prepare the task in advance; use two minutes.
• Lower standards briefly; open the task.
• Open only what you need; choose tiny action.
• Use one window; prepare first.
formula_flow: Describe Hurting → Continue Alongside → Choose Small
safety:
PAUSE
Obtain care when pain or distress needs direct treatment.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

45–60 seconds

WIN
The hurt was named honestly and one continuing process—care, learning, work, rest, or connection—received a small action.

• Make the first move tiny; lower the quality bar.
• Prepare the task in advance; use two minutes.
• Lower standards briefly; open the task.
• Open only what you need; choose tiny action.
• Use one window; prepare first.

title: GIVE THE BIG QUESTION A ROOM, NOT THE HOUSE
goal: Give a big question a limited thinking room, then return the rest of the day to living.
steps:
1. Set the Room — Choose a short time for the big question.
2. Bring One Question — Think about one clear question and stop when the time ends. You do not require a final answer.
3. Return To Life — Then do one normal task that shows how you want to live now.
win: The inquiry stopped on time without a final answer and one ordinary action resumed afterward.
supports:
• Reduce easy access to triggers; expect slips and restart quickly.
• Reset after slips; make the old habit harder.
• Change one cue; keep replacement easy.
• Change the environment first; remove easy access.
• Move the cue; interrupt the usual sequence.
formula_flow: Set the Room → Bring One Question → Return To Life
safety:
PAUSE
Seek mental health support when existential repetitive thinking impairs safety or functioning.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: NAME THE GUARANTEE YOU ARE SECRETLY BUYING
goal: Name the emotional guarantee you hope checking will buy, then ask whether data can actually sell it.
steps:
1. Finish Sentence — Finish this sentence: ‘If I keep checking, I hope to guarantee that…’ Ask whether any amount of data can provide that emotional promise.
2. Remain Demand — Gather only information that changes action; treat the remaining demand as uncertainty to carry.
win: Only information that could change action remained; the impossible guarantee was recognised as uncertainty to carry.
supports:
• Choose good enough; accept a small margin of risk.
• Choose a good-enough option; act with uncertainty.
• Delay reassurance; name what is unknown.
• Leave one question unanswered; use a decision deadline.
• Avoid reopening settled choices; accept small risk.
formula_flow: Finish Sentence → Remain Demand
safety:
PAUSE
Do not stop investigation while essential facts are still obtainable.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WHERE EXACTLY IS THE OBSERVER?
goal: Look for the observer's exact boundary and notice that every candidate location is itself observed.
steps:
1. Search Carefully — Search carefully for the boundary, size, and location of the one who observes.
2. Check Behind — Check behind the eyes, chest, head, and surrounding field.
3. Observe Found — Every found sensation is itself observed.
4. Rest Inability — Rest with the inability to locate a final point.
win: Eyes, head, chest, and surrounding field supplied sensations but no final point that could be identified as the watcher.
supports:
• Notice resentment as a warning; offer only genuine options.
• Offer alternatives only if genuine; state consequences clearly.
• Protect your capacity; delay your answer.
• Use a short no; repeat the same wording calmly.
• Let guilt pass; keep the limit simple.
formula_flow: Search Carefully → Check Behind → Observe Found → Rest Inability
safety:
PAUSE
Do not continue if location inquiry provokes feeling unreal or detached from yourself.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: PUT THE COMMENTATOR IN THE CHEAP SEAT
goal: Use real task feedback while letting self-commentary remain faint and unanswered at the edge.
steps:
1. Choose Skill — Choose one familiar, low-risk task with clear external feedback.
2. Centre Feedback — Put sight, touch, sound, or the work result in the centre of attention.
3. Demote Voice — When self-commentary appears, let it continue faintly at the edge without answering or silencing it.
4. Finish Unit — Finish one complete task unit using feedback—not self-opinion—to make corrections.
win: One work unit was corrected from sight, touch, sound, or result rather than from inner opinion.
supports:
• Park secondary tasks; keep one task visible.
• Close what you do not need; reduce nearby noise.
• Put the phone out of reach; use one screen.
• Use a short focus block; return after interruptions.
• Use one window at a time; take a short break.
formula_flow: Choose Skill → Centre Feedback → Demote Voice → Finish Unit
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if divided attention reduces accuracy or makes the activity unsafe.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE MILLISECOND BEFORE THE NAME
goal: Catch the tiny instant of contact before the mind adds name, ownership, or preference.
steps:
1. Look Touch — Look at or touch something ordinary.
2. Catch Bare — Catch the first bare instant before ‘cup,’ ‘cold,’ ownership, or preference appears.
3. Don't Freeze — Do not freeze it; simply recognise the order: contact, then concept.
4. Repeat Unnamed — Repeat with a sound.
win: An ordinary sight, touch, and sound briefly revealed the sequence of contact first and concept second.
supports:
• Notice the thought, then step back; return to the room.
• Use fewer words about it; avoid building a larger story.
• Use simple present-tense facts; drop the need to solve it.
• Do not debate every detail; reduce commentary.
• Notice where attention goes; keep one real task in view.
formula_flow: Look Touch → Catch Bare → Don't Freeze → Repeat Unnamed
safety:
PAUSE
End if preidea-based attention feels unreal or confusing.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: IMAGINE TODAY’S EMOTIONAL WEATHER
goal: Map today's emotional weather with shelter and a safe route instead of demanding sunshine.
steps:
1. Map The Weather — Imagine pressure zones, temperature, movement direction, visibility, and a likely prediction using colours or symbols.
2. Add Shelter — Add one shelter and one safe travel route.
3. Check The Shift — Revisit later to see what moved without forcing sunshine.
win: Pressure, movement, visibility, and likely direction were pictured, then later change could be noticed without forcing it.
supports:
• Check the facts separately; notice what changed physically.
• Do one steadying action; eat, drink, or rest if needed.
• Lower nearby noise; slow physical pace.
• Lower stimulation for a minute; use plain language.
• Give the feeling time to move; name the emotion.

safety:
PAUSE
Use direct crisis support when the weather includes dangerous impulses.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: SHIFT THE VIEWFINDER
goal: Find the inner camera angle that keeps the facts intact while giving you more choice.
steps:
1. Adjust — Adjust the internal scene’s distance, height, direction, and frame one at a time.
2. Test Far — Test close, far, eye-level, above, behind, wide, and cropped.
3. Choose Angle — Choose the angle that preserves facts while increasing present choice.
win: Distance, height, direction, or framing changed without changing the event itself, and one view increased present agency.
supports:
• Interrupt the sequence; make the old habit harder.
• Move the cue; add small friction.
• Reset without self-criticism; expect slips and restart quickly.
• Reduce easy access to triggers; delay the routine.
• Notice the trigger; remove easy access.

safety:

title: WHICH REGRET ARE YOU AVOIDING?
goal: Compare the regrets of acting, waiting, doing nothing, and betraying what matters.
steps:
1. Estimate Regret — For each option, estimate regret of action, inaction, delay, and self-betrayal.
2. Describe Future — Say the future scene behind the highest score.
3. Ask Regret — Ask which regret is reversible and which conflicts most with your values.
win: The most important future regret became clearer, including whether it could be repaired later.
supports:
• Use one priority; remove one conflicting commitment.
• Keep the action small; accept the trade-off.
• Choose aligned action; make the next hour reflect it.
• Keep meaning practical; check whose goal you are chasing.
• Review the cost; pick one value for this decision.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not let imagined regret override present safety or evidence.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: REMOVE WHAT THE CHOICE WOULD ‘PROVE’
goal: Remove what each option would supposedly prove about you before comparing the real consequences.
steps:
1. Say About — Name what each option would supposedly say about you—successful, loyal, brave, weak, ordinary.
2. Drop Labels — Mentally remove those identity messages from the decision.
3. Check Again — Re-check only consequences, values, constraints, and evidence.
4. Notice Shift — Notice whether the preferred option changes.
win: Status labels such as brave, weak, loyal, or successful stopped influencing the choice unless they carried actual evidence.
supports:
• Name what matters today; remove one conflict.
• Use one priority; review the cost.
• Protect important time; check whose goal you are chasing.
• Check whose goal; act before motivation.
• Make the next hour reflect it; name today's value.

title: WHOSE HANDWRITING IS ON THIS BELIEF?
goal: Trace the belief to who taught or rewarded it, then decide whether you still want to carry it.
steps:
1. Name Modelled — Name who modelled, rewarded, enforced, or normalised the belief.
2. Picture Original — Picture the original context and what compliance protected.
3. Ask Whether — Now check if current-you endorses it under present values and data.
win: The original context and protection became visible, then current values and evidence got a separate vote.
supports:
• Look for one missing fact; delay the verdict.
• Check the base rate; add the missing context.
• Use current facts; notice absolute words like always.
• Question absolute words; delay major conclusions when upset.
• Separate guess from evidence; use a real example.

safety:
PAUSE

title: CHANGE THE COMPARISON DENOMINATOR
goal: Compare yourself against a baseline with similar resources, time, responsibilities, and starting point.
steps:
1. Name Mind — Name the group your mind selected.
2. Match Resources — Substitute a baseline matched on starting point, resources, time, responsibilities, and opportunity.
3. Compare Progress — Compare progress with context included.
4. Group Exists — If no fair group exists, use your own prior trajectory.
win: Context changed the comparison, or your own prior trajectory became the fairest benchmark available.
supports:
• Notice hidden differences; track progress by your values.
• Keep context visible; do one action for your life.
• Return to your own baseline; avoid one-person benchmarks.
• Stop checking their numbers; choose your own measure.
• Use your own timeline; return to your priorities.
formula_flow: Name Mind → Match Resources → Compare Progress → Group Exists
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use context to deny areas where effort or repair is needed.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: DO ONE GOOD THING WITH NO APPLAUSE BUTTON
goal: Do one action you believe is right without announcing it or checking whether anyone approves.
steps:
1. Choose Safe — Do a low-risk act you endorse and do it without announcing, checking reactions, or fishing for extra certainty.
2. Let Discomfort — Let the discomfort of no feedback rise and change.
3. Review Quietly — Review the action by your values once it is done.
win: The act remained value-consistent even while the discomfort of receiving no feedback rose and changed.
supports:
• Leave one question unanswered; name what is unknown.
• Ask what is controllable now; choose good enough.
• Notice when checking stops helping; leave one doubt.
• Act on the safest workable option; delay reassurance.
• Set a limit on checking; use a deadline.

title: MAKE THE DOOR SMALL
goal: Reduce the task to a doorway small enough to enter now.
steps:
1. Open It — Bring the exact task to mind.
2. Aim Restarts — Choose the exact point where work can restart.
win: One exact restart point replaced the sense that the whole task had to be faced at once.
supports:
• Do the easiest useful part; choose tiny action.
• Restart quickly; begin with the easiest part.
• Open only what you need; lower the first demand.
• Lower standards briefly; prepare the task in advance.
• Reward starting, not finishing; remove one barrier.
formula_flow: Open It → Aim Restarts
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if this makes you less steady, more distressed, or less able to act safely. Use human, professional, medical, or emergency support when the situation needs more than self-help.
This brief reset is not diagnosis, treatment, or emergency care.

stepsArray: 1. Log It — Notice when too many tasks start demanding first place at once.
2. Clear Space — Hide the notifications.
3. Set Aside — Move competing demands outside this round.
tips: Finish before adding; remove duplicate work.
Protect the highest-value block; finish one before adding another.
Move low-value work later; protect one priority.
Choose the top three; match tasks to real capacity.
Add time buffer; choose top three.
mindBend: Choice overload is partly an access problem. Too many open options can flatten priority even when one choice is clearly more useful.

SINGLE-TRACK RULE

45–90 seconds

GOAL
Remove competing demands from the round so one task can genuinely hold first place.

HOW TO PLAY

2. Clear Space — Hide the notifications.
3. Set Aside — Move competing demands outside this round.

WIN
Notifications and rival tasks left the immediate field instead of continuing to demand equal priority.

• Finish before adding; remove duplicate work.
• Protect the highest-value block; finish one before adding another.
• Move low-value work later; protect one priority.
• Choose the top three; match tasks to real capacity.
• Add time buffer; choose top three.

MIND BEND
Choice overload is partly an access problem. Too many open options can flatten priority even when one choice is clearly more useful.

Log It → Clear Space → Set Aside

SAFETY
PAUSE

title: RETURN SIDE DOOR
goal: Use one small change to reveal which of the next two tasks should come first.
steps:

2. Set Order — Choose which of the next two tasks comes first.
3. Start Small — Make one small change now.
4. Close Queue — Stop when the next priority is clear.
win: The return route became clear enough that the next priority no longer needed a larger planning session.
supports:

• Move low-value work later; leave empty space.
• Cut what cannot fit; remove duplicate commitments.

title: DROP A TRAIL MARK
goal: Leave a simple trail back to unfinished work before switching away.
steps:
1. Store Handoff — Settle on one simple restart marker.
2. Move Once — Move the next task into a different physical spot.
3. Leave Trail — Picture returning to that restart point once.
win: The task moved to a distinct place and one restart marker was easy to picture on return.
supports:
• Mark your place; say the action aloud.
• Mark where you stopped; repeat last action.
• Restart from the last known point; finish one small unit.
• Reduce instructions; close unrelated tabs.
• Finish one unit; keep one next action visible.
formula_flow: Store Handoff → Move Once → Leave Trail

win: A short movement separated contexts and the new task had a single re-entry phrase ready.

title: REAL-TIME CHECK
goal: Compare the deadline with actual time and work from the visible countdown.
steps:
1. Recall Clock — Keep one honest duration.
2. Set Timer — Fix a visible countdown.
3. Take Stock — Focus on the completed part.
win: One honest duration framed the interval and the completed portion, not panic, became the result.
supports:
• Start earlier; cut scope.
• Protect breaks; start earlier than feels necessary.
• Stop adding last-minute extras; work backward.
• Choose one deadline first; check the clock.
• Protect one real break; use an external timer.
formula_flow: Recall Clock → Set Timer → Take Stock

win: Your need became a real request while the other person's answer received uninterrupted space.

goal: Keep support on your side of the delegation line and leave the actual next action with the owner.

3. Use Question — Decide on the exact point that is still unclear.

win: The request, unclear point, support, and delegated action ended in distinct places.

title: RISK UP, ASK CLEAR
goal: Raise the risk in plain language and ask the senior person for the decision it requires.
steps:
1. Bring Evidence — Name the risk in plain factual language.
2. Divide Parts — State what could happen if nothing changes.
3. Do One — Say what action or decision you need from the senior person.
4. Add Route — Offer one practical option that reduces the risk.
5. Check Meaning — Ask when the decision will be made or reviewed.
win: Consequence, requested action, mitigation option, and review timing made the escalation usable.
supports:
• Keep emotion low; confirm the agreed action.
• Use specific facts; state what you need.
• Name the decision deadline; lead with the business impact.
• Offer a workable option; state the need.
• Respect the role; avoid long background stories.

title: HEAT OFF THE ISSUE
goal: Keep the work problem separate from the person and stop sending while the surge is high.
steps:
1. Cool Pace — Slow the pace before you respond.
2. Name Evidence — Hold the visible work issue.
3. Delay Action — Stop sending during the surge.
win: The visible issue remained available without being turned into a character judgment or hot message.
supports:
• Ask for one change; name work impact.
• Take conflict private; keep facts clear.
• Delay angry replies; state the effect on work.
• Do not reply while angry; use one specific example.
• Keep the issue factual; escalate repeated patterns, not irritation.
formula_flow: Cool Pace → Name Evidence → Delay Action

• Separate guilt from responsibility; make repair smaller than self-punishment.
• Name outside factors; prefer repair.
• Recall capability; use the same standard for everyone.

title: HANDRAIL GREEN LIGHT
goal: Move toward immediate safety and human support while the panic surge is high.
steps:
1. Find Room — Move toward a calmer, safer space.
2. Ease Speed — Rest your hands on a safely cool surface.
3. Text Someone — Text a trusted person for support.
win: You reached a calmer place, used a safe physical anchor, and contacted someone who could stay with you.
supports:
• Loosen your shoulders; avoid repeated pulse checking.
• Reduce caffeine; keep movements gentle.
• Reduce extra stimulation; unclench your jaw.
• Keep your body supported; sip water if it helps.
• Sit somewhere safe; wait out the surge.
formula_flow: Find Room → Ease Speed → Text Someone
safety:
PAUSE
Keep your eyes open and orient to the room. Stop if symptoms intensify, you feel faint, or a medical problem may be possible. Call Triple Zero (000) for an emergency; otherwise use qualified medical advice. Do not induce or test symptoms.
This is brief self-help, not diagnosis or treatment.

title: COOL FIRST, SEND SECOND
goal: Keep only the boundary or request that remains true after the angry rush is separated from it.
steps:
1. Postpone Move — Pause before you send anything.
2. Slow Hands — Name the physical rush in one compact sentence.
3. Split Facts — Compare the angry prediction with one current fact.
4. Keep Edge — Keep only the factual boundary or request you still stand by.
5. Say Simply — Send nothing until you can say it in the shortest honest sentence without a threat or insult.
win: The message stayed unsent until the factual part could be expressed briefly without threat or insult.
supports:
• Drop old grievances; delay the message.
• Stick to facts; leave the argument.
• Lower your voice on purpose; return when your body settles.
• Stick to current facts; use one request.
• Avoid empty threats; name the exact issue.
formula_flow: Postpone Move → Slow Hands → Split Facts → Keep Edge → Say Simply
safety:
PAUSE
Do not send, drive, confront, threaten, or act while control feels reduced. Move away from weapons and hazards; use human or emergency support if anyone may be unsafe.
This is brief self-help, not treatment or emergency care.

goal: End self-investigation and move toward a familiar person or staffed safe place.
steps:
1. Pause All Rituals — End the self-help session and do not investigate the experience further.
2. Find Familiar Support — Move toward a familiar person or a staffed, safe place.
3. Describe One Concern — Describe one concrete concern without debating its meaning.
4. Use Crisis Contact — Call the appropriate Australian service listed in Safety.
5. Keep Company — Do not remain alone while urgent support is being arranged.
win: The experience was described concretely, Australian support was contacted, and you did not remain alone while help was arranged.
supports:
• Keep a trusted person nearby.
• Reduce noise and stimulation.
• Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs.
• Say exactly what you are noticing.
• Contact a mental-health professional today.

title: CLOSE THE DECISION LOOP
goal: End the reopened choice by separating intended effect from actual result and finishing one active piece.
steps:
1. Make Cue — Say one sentence aloud.
2. Unmix Story — Describe the difference between the intended effect and what really happened.
3. Park Rest — Pin down which questions can stay parked.
4. Begin Now — Complete one finishable piece of the active task.
5. Set Ending — Say where this loop can stop.
win: Parked questions remained parked, one task piece was completed, and you named exactly where to stop.
supports:
• Choose reversible first; stop researching after enough evidence.
• Ask what failure would cost; commit once chosen.
• Name the non-negotiables; stop extra research.
• Accept one trade-off; use strongest evidence.
• Choose the option you can support; set a decision deadline.

title: FACT QUICK-TURN
goal: Keep uncertainty separate from the visible result instead of letting each stand in for the other.
steps:
1. Name Unknown — Say the uncertain piece.
2. Take Stock — State the visible result a single time.
win: The unknown part and the observable outcome were each stated once without being fused.
supports:
• Delay reassurance seeking; choose a good-enough option.
• Leave one doubt; ask what is controllable now.
• Name what is known; accept a small margin of risk.
• Stop reopening choices; notice when checking stops helping.
• Choose good enough; act with uncertainty.
